claim: Mice lacking the dopamine D1 receptor (D1R KO mice) manifest greatly reduced food anticipatory activity (FAA).
source: In this study, we show that mice lacking the dopamine D1 receptor (D1R KO mice) manifest greatly reduced FAA, whereas mice lacking the dopamine D2 receptor have normal FAA.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2-9.

claim: Mice lacking the dopamine D2 receptor have normal food anticipatory activity (FAA).
source: In this study, we show that mice lacking the dopamine D1 receptor (D1R KO mice) manifest greatly reduced FAA, whereas mice lacking the dopamine D2 receptor have normal FAA.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Dopamine-deficient mice with dopamine signaling limited to the dorsal striatum developed FAA.
source: To determine where dopamine exerts its effect, we limited expression of dopamine signaling to the dorsal striatum of dopamine-deficient mice; these mice developed FAA.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 10.

claim: The daily rhythm of clock gene period2 expression was markedly suppressed in the dorsal striatum of D1R KO mice.
source: Within the dorsal striatum, the daily rhythm of clock gene period2 expression was markedly suppressed in D1R KO mice.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 11.

claim: Pharmacological activation of D1R at the same time daily was sufficient to establish anticipatory activity in wild-type mice.
source: Pharmacological activation of D1R at the same time daily was sufficient to establish anticipatory activity in wild-type mice.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 12.

claim: Dopamine signaling to D1R-expressing neurons in the dorsal striatum plays an important role in manifestation of FAA.
source: These results demonstrate that dopamine signaling to D1R-expressing neurons in the dorsal striatum plays an important role in manifestation of FAA, possibly by synchronizing circadian oscillators that modulate motivational processes and behavioral output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: D1R signaling may synchronize circadian oscillators that modulate motivational processes and behavioral output.
source: These results demonstrate that dopamine signaling to D1R-expressing neurons in the dorsal striatum plays an important role in manifestation of FAA, possibly by synchronizing circadian oscillators that modulate motivational processes and behavioral output.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Daily rhythms of food anticipatory activity (FAA) are regulated independently of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
source: Daily rhythms of food anticipatory activity (FAA) are regulated independently of the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which mediates entrainment of rhythms to light, but the neural circuits that establish FAA remain elusive.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) mediates entrainment of rhythms to light.
source: Daily rhythms of food anticipatory activity (FAA) are regulated independently of the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which mediates entrainment of rhythms to light, but the neural circuits that establish FAA remain elusive.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the SCN's role in circadian rhythms.

claim: The neural circuits that establish FAA remain elusive.
source: Daily rhythms of food anticipatory activity (FAA) are regulated independently of the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which mediates entrainment of rhythms to light, but the neural circuits that establish FAA remain elusive.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Circadian rhythms of behavior and physiology are regulated by a distributed system of cell-autonomous circadian oscillators located in the brain and in most peripheral organs and tissues.
source: Circadian (∼24 hr) rhythms of behavior and physiology are regulated by a distributed system of cell-autonomous circadian oscillators located in the brain and in most peripheral organs and tissues (Bell-Pedersen et al., 2005; Mohawk et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A population of coupled circadian clock cells in the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) function as a master pacemaker responsible for coordinating circadian oscillators elsewhere in the brain and other tissues with daily light–dark cycles.
source: In mammals, a population of coupled circadian clock cells in the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) function as a master pacemaker responsible for coordinating circadian oscillators elsewhere in the brain and other tissues with daily light–dark cycles (Welsh et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Circadian clocks in many tissues, including multiple brain regions outside of the SCN, can be entrained by daily cycles of food availability, independently of the SCN pacemaker.
source: Circadian clocks in many tissues, including multiple brain regions outside of the SCN, can also be entrained by daily cycles of food availability, independently of the SCN pacemaker (Stokkan et al., 2001; Mistlberger, 2011; Verwey and Amir, 2011; Mohawk et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Restricting food access to the middle of the light period in rats and mice induces a marked shifting of circadian oscillators and organ functions to align with the new daily feeding time, while the SCN remains coupled to the light-dark cycle.
source: In rat and mouse, this is readily demonstrated by restricting food access to the middle of the light period, when nocturnal rodents normally eat little and are inactive. This induces a marked shifting of circadian oscillators and organ functions to align with the new daily feeding time, while the SCN remains coupled to the light-dark (LD) cycle.
evidence: This statement describes established experimental observations in the field.

claim: Restricting food access to the middle of the light period in many species is associated with the emergence of a daily bout of locomotor activity that anticipates meal time by 1–3 hr.
source: In many species, this is also associated with the emergence of a daily bout of locomotor activity that anticipates meal time by 1–3 hr (Boulos and Terman, 1980; Stephan, 2002; Mistlberger, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Food anticipatory activity (FAA) exhibits formal properties of circadian clock control.
source: Remarkably, this so-called food anticipatory activity (FAA) exhibits formal properties of circadian clock control, yet persists robustly after removal of the SCN (Stephan et al., 1979; Boulos and Terman, 1980; Marchant and Mistlberger, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Food anticipatory activity (FAA) persists robustly after removal of the SCN.
source: Remarkably, this so-called food anticipatory activity (FAA) exhibits formal properties of circadian clock control, yet persists robustly after removal of the SCN (Stephan et al., 1979; Boulos and Terman, 1980; Marchant and Mistlberger, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Anticipatory rhythms can be induced by scheduled daily access to water, salt, palatable foods, an opportunity to mate, and psychostimulant drugs.
source: Anticipatory rhythms can also be induced by scheduled daily access to water, salt, palatable foods, an opportunity to mate, and psychostimulant drugs (Mistlberger and Rusak, 1987; Mistlberger, 1994; Kosobud et al., 1998; Iijima et al., 2002; Mendoza et al., 2005; Honma and Honma, 2009; Webb et al., 2009; Hsu et al., 2010a, 2010b; Gallardo et al., 2012; Jansen et al., 2012; Landry et al., 2012; Mohawk et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ability of animals to coordinate activity and physiology with access to critical resources is adaptive.
source: The ability of animals to coordinate activity and physiology with access to critical resources is obviously adaptive.
evidence: This is a general inference based on evolutionary principles.

claim: Similar circadian processes in humans could create daily windows of vulnerability to drug seeking, overeating, and other addictive behaviors.
source: Similar circadian processes in humans could create daily windows of vulnerability to drug seeking, overeating, and other addictive behaviors.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from animal studies to human behavior.

claim: A major knowledge gap in circadian neurobiology is the location of circadian oscillators that generate food (and other reward) anticipatory circadian rhythms.
source: A major knowledge gap in circadian neurobiology is the location of circadian oscillators that generate food (and other reward) anticipatory circadian rhythms.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The stimuli and neural pathways that entrain food-entrainable oscillators remain unspecified.
source: The stimuli and neural pathways that entrain these oscillators also remain unspecified.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Conventional lesion experiments have ruled out a number of brain regions as the site of circadian oscillators necessary for FAA.
source: Conventional lesion experiments have ruled out a number of brain regions as the site of circadian oscillators necessary for FAA (Mistlberger, 1994, 2011; Davidson, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The dorsomedial nucleus of the hypothalamus may participate in the expression of daytime FAA by inhibiting output from the SCN pacemaker that normally opposes activity and promotes rest during the day in nocturnal rodents.
source: This includes the dorsomedial nucleus of the hypothalamus, an area that may nonetheless participate in the expression of daytime FAA by inhibiting output from the SCN pacemaker that normally opposes activity and promotes rest during the day in nocturnal rodents (Acosta-Galvan et al., 2011; Landry et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Induction of anticipatory rhythms by a range of ingestive and non-ingestive reward stimuli suggest that activation of reward circuits in the brain may play a role, perhaps as a final common entrainment pathway.
source: Induction of anticipatory rhythms by a range of ingestive and non-ingestive reward stimuli suggest that activation of reward circuits in the brain may play a role, perhaps as a final common entrainment pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior observations.

claim: Circadian clock genes exhibit daily rhythms of expression in components of the reward system, including the dorsal striatum and nucleus accumbens.
source: This is supported by evidence that circadian clock genes exhibit daily rhythms of expression in components of the reward system, including the dorsal striatum and nucleus accumbens (Wakamatsu et al., 2001; Angeles-Castellanos et al., 2007; Verwey and Amir, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Daily rhythms of clock gene expression in the dorsal striatum and nucleus accumbens are inverted by daytime feeding.
source: These rhythms are inverted by daytime feeding, and, in the dorsal striatum, can be induced or reset by dopaminergic stimuli (Iijima et al., 2002; Hood et al., 2010; Natsubori et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Daily rhythms of clock gene expression in the dorsal striatum can be induced or reset by dopaminergic stimuli.
source: These rhythms are inverted by daytime feeding, and, in the dorsal striatum, can be induced or reset by dopaminergic stimuli (Iijima et al., 2002; Hood et al., 2010; Natsubori et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FAA rhythms can be shifted by a single injection of a dopamine D2 receptor agonist.
source: Importantly, FAA rhythms can be shifted by a single injection of a dopamine D2 receptor agonist (Smit et al., 2013) and can be attenuated by dopamine D1 and D2 antagonists (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FAA rhythms can be attenuated by dopamine D1 and D2 antagonists.
source: Importantly, FAA rhythms can be shifted by a single injection of a dopamine D2 receptor agonist (Smit et al., 2013) and can be attenuated by dopamine D1 and D2 antagonists (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Genetic deletion of factors that activate dopamine transmission (e.g., ghrelin receptors) can attenuate FAA.
source: In addition, genetic deletion of factors that activate dopamine transmission (e.g., ghrelin receptors) can attenuate FAA (Blum et al., 2009; LeSauter et al., 2009; Lamont et al., 2012), but see (Szentirmai et al., 2010; Gunapala et al., 2011; Patton et al., 2013) while deletion of factors that suppress DA transmission (e.g., leptin and 5HT1c receptors) can increase FAA (Mistlberger and Marchant, 1999; Hsu et al., 2010c; Ribeiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research, with some conflicting results noted.

claim: Deletion of factors that suppress dopamine transmission (e.g., leptin and 5HT1c receptors) can increase FAA.
source: In addition, genetic deletion of factors that activate dopamine transmission (e.g., ghrelin receptors) can attenuate FAA (Blum et al., 2009; LeSauter et al., 2009; Lamont et al., 2012), but see (Szentirmai et al., 2010; Gunapala et al., 2011; Patton et al., 2013) while deletion of factors that suppress DA transmission (e.g., leptin and 5HT1c receptors) can increase FAA (Mistlberger and Marchant, 1999; Hsu et al., 2010c; Ribeiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lesion experiments rule out the nucleus accumbens as the site of dopamine receptors that might be necessary for FAA.
source: Lesion experiments rule out the nucleus accumbens as the site of dopamine receptors that might be necessary for FAA (Mistlberger and Mumby, 1992), but comparable experiments of the dorsal striatum have not been reported.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Comparable lesion experiments of the dorsal striatum have not been reported.
source: Lesion experiments rule out the nucleus accumbens as the site of dopamine receptors that might be necessary for FAA (Mistlberger and Mumby, 1992), but comparable experiments of the dorsal striatum have not been reported.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: D2R WT and KO mice demonstrated normal nocturnal activity waveforms with no significant differences in any 1-hr bin and no increase in activity in the hours before ZT 8 on day -7 prior to dietary intervention.
source: Prior to any dietary intervention ('day -7'), both groups of mice demonstrated normal nocturnal activity waveforms with no significant differences in any 1-hr bin and no increase in activity in the hours before Zeitgeber Time (ZT) 8 (on a 13:11 LD cycle, ZT 12 is lights-off by convention) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Both D2R WT and KO mice had a large increase in high activity behaviors during the 3 hr preceding feeding time at 14, 21, and 28 days of CR.
source: Measurements taken at 14, 21, and 28 days of CR revealed that both WT and D2R KO mice had a large increase in high activity (hanging, jumping, walking, and rearing) behaviors during the 3 hr preceding feeding time (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claim: D2R KO and WT mice fed 60% CR daily showed similar acquisition and maintenance of FAA.
source: In both D2R KO and WT mice fed 60% CR daily, we observed similar acquisition and maintenance of FAA defined as normalized high activity in the 3 hr before feeding (ZT 5–8) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: D2R KO and WT mice with ad libitum access to food showed very little high activity behavior in the hours preceding scheduled feeding when given an additional food pellet as a control for handling and disturbance.
source: As expected, mice of either genotype with ad libitum (AL) access to food showed very little high activity behavior in the hours preceding scheduled feeding when they were given an additional food pellet as a control for handling and disturbance (Figure 1F).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: D2R is not necessary for mediating FAA on a 60% CR meal.
source: These results suggest that D2R is not necessary for mediating FAA on a 60% CR meal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: D1R KO mice showed slightly increased nocturnal activity compared to WT controls prior to dietary intervention on day -7.
source: The normalized activity waveform of D1R WT and D1R KO mice prior to any dietary intervention on day -7 revealed strong nocturnal activity in D1R KO and control mice, with D1R KO mice showing slightly increased nocturnal activity compared to WT controls (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: D1R KO mice had a median value of 173.8 min of high activity behaviors in the 11 hr of dark, compared to 93.5 min for D1R WT mice, which was statistically significant (p = 0.045).
source: Summation of time of high activity behaviors in the 11 hr of dark yielded a median value of 93.5 min (min) for D1R WT mice (n = 16) compared with a value of 173.8 min for D1R KO (n = 19); this difference was statistically significant (p = 0.045, Mann–Whitney Test).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Activity values during the lights-on period were not significantly different between D1R KO and WT mice (median values of 44.2 and 51.3 min, respectively; p = 0.46).
source: In comparison, activity values during the lights-on period were not significantly different (median values of 44.2 and 51.3 min were observed for D1R WT and KO, respectively; p = 0.46)
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: D1R KO mice do not exhibit locomotor defects preventing nocturnal activity.
source: These results suggest that the D1R KO mice do not exhibit locomotor defects preventing nocturnal activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that D1R KO mice show normal or increased nocturnal activity.

claim: D1R WT mice showed notable increase in activity preceding scheduled meal time by 14 days of CR while D1R KO mice showed only a small increase in activity.
source: When placed on a timed 60% CR feeding schedule with a ZT 8 meal time, D1R WT mice showed notable increase in activity preceding scheduled meal time by 14 days of CR while D1R KO mice showed only a small increase in activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: On day 21 of CR, WT control mice exhibited a significant (p < 0.05) increase in high activity compared to D1R KO mice in ZT 6 and 7.
source: On day 21 of CR, WT control mice exhibited a significant (p < 0.05) increase in high activity compared to D1R KO mice in ZT 6 and 7 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: On day 28 of CR, WT mice showed a significantly higher (p < 0.01) fraction of high activity in each hourly bin from ZT 5–7 compared to D1R KO mice.
source: This was observed again on day 28 with WT mice showing a significantly higher (p < 0.01) fraction of high activity in each hourly bin from ZT 5–7 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: D1R KO mice had a stable and significant impairment in FAA (p < 0.01 at day 14, p < 0.001 at days 21 and 28) from day 14 of scheduled feeding onwards.
source: Summation of the amount of normalized high activity in the 3 hr preceding scheduled meal access revealed that D1R KO mice had a stable and significant impairment in FAA (p < 0.01 at day 14, p < 0.001 at days 21 and 28) from day 14 of scheduled feeding onwards (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: D1R WT control mice on an AL diet showed a small increase in activity relative to D1R KO mice on day 7.
source: As expected, both D1R KO and WT mice with AL access to food showed very little normalized high activity behaviors in ZT 5–8 with the exception of day 7 when D1R WT control mice showed a small increase in activity relative to D1R KO mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: D1R KO mice had reduced overall activity on a 60% CR diet after day 14.
source: We also plotted the median time (in seconds) of high activity in D1R KO and WT mice over the course of 28 days of CR and observed that D1R KO mice had reduced overall activity on a 60% CR diet after day 14 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: During AL food access, activity measured by running discs and motion sensors was nearly indistinguishable in amount and timing (% nocturnality) in D1R KO and WT groups.
source: During AL food access, activity measured by running discs and motion sensors was nearly indistinguishable in amount and timing (% nocturnality) in the KO and WT groups (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 3A and 3D.

claim: When food was gradually restricted to a 4-hr daily meal for 32 days, WT mice exhibited a bout of disc running that began ∼2 hr prior to meal time and increased monotonically to a peak at meal time within a few days.
source: When food (powdered chow mixed with corn oil 20% by weight) was gradually restricted to a 4-hr daily meal for 32 days, beginning at ZT 6 (6 hr after lights-on), WT mice exhibited a bout of disc running that began ∼2 hr prior to meal time and increased monotonically to a peak at meal time within a few days (Figure 3B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Total daily running did not change in WT mice during restricted feeding.
source: Total daily running did not change.
evidence: This statement is based on the data presented in the study.

claim: Relative to WT mice, D1R KO mice exhibited significantly less total daily running during food restriction, and a marked reduction in FAA, expressed both as 2-hr total counts and as a ratio relative to activity during the rest of the day, excluding meal time (p < 0.05).
source: Relative to WT mice, D1R KO mice exhibited significantly less total daily running during food restriction, and a marked reduction in FAA, expressed both as 2-hr total counts and as a ratio relative to activity during the rest of the day, excluding meal time (p < 0.05; Figure 3E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: D1R KO mice weighed significantly less than WT mice prior to restricted feeding (15.2 ± 2.6 g vs 23.3 ± 2.3 g, p < 0.001).
source: KO mice weighed significantly less than WT mice prior to restricted feeding (15.2 ± 2.6 g vs 23.3 ± 2.3 g, p < 0.001) and showed equivalent changes in weight across the 32 days of restricted feeding, losing ∼15% body weight over the first week, regaining this by the end of the second week, and remaining stable until day 32 (weight as a percent of baseline = 96 ± 3% vs 105 ± 7% in WT vs KO, respectively, p = 0.22).
evidence: This statement is supported by weight measurements during the experiment.

claim: D1R KO and WT mice showed equivalent changes in weight across the 32 days of restricted feeding, losing ∼15% body weight over the first week, regaining this by the end of the second week, and remaining stable until day 32.
source: KO mice weighed significantly less than WT mice prior to restricted feeding (15.2 ± 2.6 g vs 23.3 ± 2.3 g, p < 0.001) and showed equivalent changes in weight across the 32 days of restricted feeding, losing ∼15% body weight over the first week, regaining this by the end of the second week, and remaining stable until day 32 (weight as a percent of baseline = 96 ± 3% vs 105 ± 7% in WT vs KO, respectively, p = 0.22).
evidence: This statement is supported by weight measurements during the experiment.

claim: When the diet was changed to powdered chow mixed with water, D1R KO mice continued to show significantly less total activity (p < 0.01) and less FAA (p < 0.01) than WT mice.
source: To determine if the palatability or caloric density of the food influences the magnitude of FAA differentially in KO and WT mice, the diet was changed to powdered chow mixed with water. The mice were fed ad-lib for 22 days and were then restricted to a 4-hr daily meal for 74 days. KO mice continued to show significantly less total activity (p < 0.01) and less FAA (p < 0.01) than WT mice.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the experiment with regular chow.

claim: FAA ratios in both D1R KO and WT groups were increased relative to the ratios evident when fed high fat chow, but remained significantly lower in KO mice (p < 0.05).
source: FAA ratios in both groups were increased relative to the ratios evident when fed high fat chow, but remained significantly lower in KO mice (p < 0.05).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the experiment with regular chow.

claim: In only one D1R KO mouse were the FAA counts and the FAA ratios significantly increased during the last 10 days of restricted feeding compared to the last 10 days of ad-lib food access.
source: In only one KO mice were the FAA counts and the FAA ratios significantly increased during the last 10 days of restricted feeding compared to the last 10 days of ad-lib food access (counts: paired t(9) = 6.52, p < 0.001; ratios t(9) = 5.22, p = 0.005), whereas the counts and ratios were significantly increased in all of the WT mice at p < 0.00001.
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Differences between D1R KO and WT mice in FAA were stable across 74 days on the restricted feeding schedule with regular chow.
source: Differences between KO and WT mice were stable across 74 days on this restricted feeding schedule.
evidence: This statement is based on the data presented in the study.

claim: Body weights remained stable at ∼90% of baseline in both D1R KO and WT groups during restricted feeding with regular chow.
source: Body weights remained stable at ∼90% of baseline in both groups.
evidence: This statement is based on weight measurements during the experiment.

claim: D1R KO mice failed to show FAA for breeder chow, exerting only 4–8% of their total daily high activity behaviors in the 3 hr preceding scheduled meal time.
source: D1R KO mice failed to show FAA for breeder chow, exerting only 4–8% of their total daily high activity behaviors in the 3 hr preceding scheduled meal time (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: WT mice showed FAA for breeder chow, but it was attenuated compared to that observed with standard chow, as WT mice redistributed only ∼20% of high activity behaviors to the 3 hr preceding feeding compared to 30–40% on standard chow.
source: Interestingly, although WT mice showed FAA for breeder chow, it was attenuated compared to that observed with standard chow, as WT mice redistributed only ∼20% of high activity behaviors to the 3 hr preceding feeding (Figure 4A,C) compared to 30–40% on standard chow (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 4A, 4C, and 2E.

claim: A 60% CR diet of HFD fed once daily at ZT 8 failed to induce FAA in D1R KO mice and induced a very modest FAA in WT controls, which allocated only about 10% of total high activity behaviors to the 3 hr preceding meal time.
source: We also tested an even higher fat content chow, rodent 'high fat diet' (HFD), in which 60% of the calories come from fat. A 60% CR diet of HFD fed once daily at ZT 8 failed to induce FAA in D1R KO mice and induced a very modest FAA in WT controls, which allocated only about 10% of total high activity behaviors to the 3 hr preceding meal time (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 4B and 4D.

claim: D1R KO mice do not fail to anticipate scheduled meal time due to a lack of palatability of the CR food source.
source: From these experiments, we concluded that D1R KO mice do not fail to anticipate scheduled meal time due to a lack of palatability of the CR food source.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with different diets.

claim: D1R KO mice showed a strong increase in high-activity behaviors upon acute food deprivation, increasing their activity to a greater extent than fasted WT mice, with mean values of 270.5 min and 376.9 min of high activity, respectively.
source: D1R KO mice showed a strong increase in high-activity behaviors upon acute food deprivation, increasing their activity to a greater extent than fasted WT mice, with mean values of 270.5 min and 376.9 min of high activity, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When food deprived, D1R WT mice had an activity ratio of 1.9 and D1R KO mice had a ratio of 2.5 (both statistically significant when compared within genotype to AL, p < 0.01).
source: However, when food deprived, WT mice had an activity ratio of 1.9 and D1R KO mice had a ratio of 2.5 (both of which were statistically significant when compared within genotype to AL, p < 0.01 Mann–Whitney).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: D1R KO mice are capable of up-regulating activity in response to acute food deprivation (i.e., hunger), demonstrating an intact circuitry of detecting and responding to fasting and thus ruling out gross metabolic defects.
source: These results suggest that the D1R KO mice are capable of up-regulating activity in response to acute food deprivation (i.e., hunger), demonstrating an intact circuitry of detecting and responding to fasting and thus ruling out gross metabolic defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the acute fasting experiment.

claim: D1R KO mice on a CR diet did not show a sustained increase in activity after being cued to feeding time; their activity lasted only ∼10 min subsequent to the cue.
source: D1R KO mice on a CR diet did not show a sustained increase in activity after being cued to feeding time; their activity lasted only ∼10 min subsequent to the cue (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: WT control mice on a CR diet showed a large increase in activity induced by the cue, or were already demonstrating FAA at the time of the cue, and sustained their increased activity for the following 2 hr.
source: WT control mice on a CR diet showed a large increase in activity induced by the cue, or were already demonstrating FAA at the time of the cue, and sustained their increased activity for the following 2 hr (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Summation of the time of high-activity behavior 2 hr prior to feeding demonstrated a significant increase in activity in WT mice when CR compared to AL feeding, but not in D1R KO mice.
source: Summation of the time of high-activity behavior 2 hr prior to feeding demonstrated a significant increase in activity in WT mice when CR compared to AL feeding, but not in D1R KO mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cuing the D1R KO mice to the subsequent availability of food did not trigger FAA behaviors.
source: These results suggest that even cuing the D1R KO mice to the subsequent availability of food did not trigger FAA behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cuing experiment.

claim: D1R KO mice approached the HFD meal placed in their food bin immediately and started consuming it avidly.
source: D1R KO mice, which often fail to eat from the wire food bin and need to be fed their standard chow on the cage floor, approached the HFD meal placed in their food bin immediately and started consuming it avidly.
evidence: This is an observation from the palatable meal experiment.

claim: Both D1R WT and KO mice consumed their HFD meal in less than 1 hr, spending 10% of their food-bin entry time during the hour after palatable-diet feeding.
source: Both WT and D1R KO mice consumed their HFD meal in less than 1 hr, spending 10% of their food-bin entry time during the hour after palatable-diet feeding (Figure 7A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Preprandial food-bin entry was elevated in D1R KO mice by ZT 8 on the 14th day of scheduled palatable meals.
source: We noted that preprandial food-bin entry, a hallmark of HFD meal entrainment (Hsu et al., 2010b), was elevated in D1R KO mice by ZT 8 on the 14th day of scheduled palatable meals (Figure 7B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: On day 14 of scheduled palatable meals, both D1R KO and WT groups of mice exhibited similar activity patterns over the course of the day, with small, but similar, increases in activity preceding their HFD meal.
source: On day 14, both groups of mice exhibited similar activity patterns over the course of the day, with small, but similar, increases in activity preceding their HFD meal (Figure 7C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Summing high activity in the 3 hr prior to feeding (ZT 6–9) shows a similar trend of increased fraction of high activity after 10 days of HFD meal treatment for both D1R KO and control mice.
source: Summing high activity in the 3 hr prior to feeding (ZT 6–9) shows a similar trend of increased fraction of high activity after 10 days of HFD meal treatment for both D1R KO and control mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Daily HFD meals elicited modest FAA in D1R KO mice.
source: Given how poorly D1R KO mice expressed FAA for 60% CR meals, it is surprising that daily HFD meals elicited even modest FAA, leading us to retest FAA for 60% CR meals in the same cohort of mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the palatable meal experiment.

claim: After just 1 week ('day 28') of 60% CR following HFD pre-treatment, the D1R KO mice showed marked FAA for their daily feeding, with a notable FAA peak that was as high as the night time activity peak.
source: However, after just 1 week ('day 28') of 60% CR, the D1R KO mice that had previously been treated with HFD showed marked FAA for their daily feeding, with a notable FAA peak that was as high as the night time activity peak (Figure 8B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: There was no significant difference between the amount of FAA exhibited between D1R KO and WT mice on day 28 following HFD pre-treatment (p = 0.734).
source: There was no significant difference between the amount of FAA exhibited between D1R KO and WT mice on day 28 (p = 0.734, Mann–Whitney).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: By the 14th day of 60% CR ('day 35' of the experiment) following HFD pre-treatment, the D1R KO mice no longer showed FAA and the difference with control mice was highly significant (p = 0.0003).
source: Remarkably, by the 14th day of 60% CR ('day 35' of the experiment), the D1R KO mice no longer showed FAA (Figure 8D,G) and the difference with control mice was highly significant (p = 0.0003, Mann–Whitney).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 8D and 8G.

claim: The lack of FAA in D1R KO mice persisted through days 42 and 49 following HFD pre-treatment, whereas control mice maintained on a CR diet continued to express robust FAA.
source: This lack of FAA in D1R KO mice persisted through days 42 and 49, whereas control mice maintained on a CR diet continued to express robust FAA (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 8E and 8F.

claim: WT mice showed significant differences between FAA observed at day 22 and days 28, 35, 42, and 49 following HFD pre-treatment, whereas D1R KO mice only showed significant differences in FAA between day 22 and day 28 but not any other day.
source: We performed a Kruskal–Wallis test to determine whether there were significant within-genotype variations in this experiment and found that WT mice showed significant differences between FAA observed at day 22 and days 28, 35, 42, and 49, whereas D1R KO mice only showed significant differences in FAA between day 22 and day 28 but not any other day, indicating that the D1R KO mice transiently up-regulate FAA whereas control mice sustain this increase.
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: D1R KO mice transiently up-regulate FAA whereas control mice sustain this increase following HFD pre-treatment.
source: We performed a Kruskal–Wallis test to determine whether there were significant within-genotype variations in this experiment and found that WT mice showed significant differences between FAA observed at day 22 and days 28, 35, 42, and 49, whereas D1R KO mice only showed significant differences in FAA between day 22 and day 28 but not any other day, indicating that the D1R KO mice transiently up-regulate FAA whereas control mice sustain this increase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis.

claim: D1R-mediated signaling is not absolutely required for FAA.
source: We conclude that D1R-mediated signaling is not absolutely required for FAA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that D1R KO mice can transiently show FAA following HFD pre-treatment.

claim: Visual observations at meal time provided no evidence for torpor in D1R KO mice.
source: Visual observations at meal time provided no evidence for torpor in D1R KO mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: D1R KO and WT mice placed at 30°C continuously did not show FAA after 1 week at 30°C and 4 weeks of 60% CR, with a marked reduction in FAA for the WT mice at this elevated temperature compared to ambient (22–24°C) temperature.
source: To rule out defects in thermoregulation as a reason why D1R KO mice do not show FAA, we placed D1R KO (n = 7) and WT (n = 7) mice at 30°C continuously. After 1 week at 30°C, we tested their behavioral response to 60% CR for the next 4 weeks and did not observe FAA in D1R KO mice and noted a marked reduction in FAA for the WT mice at this elevated temperature compared to ambient (22–24°C) temperature (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 24-hr body temperature profiles showed identical waveforms for D1R WT and KO groups before CR schedules were started ('day -3') with temperatures remaining close to 34.5°C during the daytime and increasing to up to ∼36°C at night-time.
source: The 24-hr body temperature profiles showed identical waveforms for WT and KO groups before CR schedules were started ('day -3') with temperatures remaining close to 34.5°C during the daytime and increasing to up to ∼36°C at night-time (Figure 9A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: By day 14 of CR, there was a similar redistribution of mean temperature waveforms in both D1R KO and WT mice, starting with a slightly elevated postprandial temperatures and steady temperature declines in the middle of the dark phase (ZT 19) that continues until about 6 hr before expected meal time.
source: By day 14 of CR, there was a similar redistribution of mean temperature waveforms in both D1R KO and WT mice, starting with a slightly elevated postprandial temperatures and steady temperature declines in the middle of the dark phase (ZT 19) that continues until about 6 hr before expected meal time (Figure 9B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: D1R KO mice tended to show a slightly higher temperature during the entirety of the dark cycle compared to WT controls during CR.
source: Despite similar profiles in temperature waveforms, we did note that D1R KO mice tended to show a slightly higher temperature during the entirety of the dark cycle compared to WT controls during CR (Figure 9B–D, Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 9B-D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no statistically significant differences in nocturnal temperature between D1R WT and KO (genotype accounts for 5.63% of the total variance; F = 1.15; p = 0.3044) but there was a significant effect of day of experiment (interaction accounts for 4.43% of the total variance; F = 4.53; p = 0.0001; 2-way repeated measures ANOVA).
source: We tested for an effect of genotype and day of measurement on nocturnal temperature, finding that there were no statistically significant differences between D1R WT and KO (genotype accounts for 5.63% of the total variance; F = 1.15; p = 0.3044) but there was a significant effect of day of experiment (interaction accounts for 4.43% of the total variance; F = 4.53; p = 0.0001; 2-way repeated measures ANOVA).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the temperature data.

claim: There was no significant difference in average temperatures between D1R KO and controls during the 3 hr preceding feeding at any point during the experiment.
source: However, there was no significant difference in average temperatures between D1R KO and controls during the 3 hr preceding feeding at any point during the experiment (Figure 9E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: D1R KO and WT mice show increasing ΔT following the start of CR feeding schedules with values peaking by day 7.
source: By this metric, D1R KO and WT mice show increasing ΔT following the start of CR feeding schedules with values peaking by day 7 (Figure 9F).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: The D1R KO mice had a similar ΔT to control at all times except for days 14 and 17, where this difference was statistically significant (p < 0.05, day 17).
source: The D1R KO mice had a similar ΔT to control at all times except for days 14 and 17, where this difference was statistically significant (p < 0.05, day 17).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Overall there are subtle differences in temperature entrainment in D1R KO mice but overall their metabolism is effectively modulated by CR feeding; importantly, they do not fail to show FAA due to entering a torpor state.
source: Given that the ΔT is similar again by day 21, we conclude that overall there are subtle differences in temperature entrainment in D1R KO mice but that overall their metabolism is effectively modulated by CR feeding; importantly, they do not fail to show FAA due to entering a torpor state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temperature data.

claim: CAV-inoculated dopamine-deficient mice showed expression of dopamine restricted to neurons that innervate the dorsolateral striatum.
source: CAV-inoculated mice showed expression of dopamine restricted to neurons that innervate the dorsolateral striatum (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 10A and 10B.

claim: Quantitative analysis of the TH staining revealed a significant difference in restoration when comparing dorsal vs ventral striatum or anterior commissure (aca) (p = 0.018, Kruskal–Wallis test).
source: Quantitative analysis of the TH straining revealed a significant difference in restoration when comparing dorsal vs ventral striatum or anterior commissure (aca), which is always devoid of TH staining (p = 0.018, Kruskal–Wallis test; p = 0.0486 comparing dorsal vs ventral, p = 0.0112 for dorsal vs aca, and p = 0.999 for ventral vs aca, Dunn's post-test for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the TH staining data.

claim: Initially the activity waveforms of the DD-VR mice showed a trend toward increased activity at night.
source: Initially the activity waveforms of the DD-VR mice showed a trend toward increased activity at night (Figure 10B), and they did not show appreciable FAA at the 7-day-time point (p < 0.05) (Figure 10C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: DD-VR mice did not show appreciable FAA at the 7-day-time point (p < 0.05).
source: Initially the activity waveforms of the DD-VR mice showed a trend toward increased activity at night (Figure 10B), and they did not show appreciable FAA at the 7-day-time point (p < 0.05) (Figure 10C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: By day 14 and onwards DD-VR mice showed a strong FAA response, eventually having almost all of their daily activity preceding meal time as did sham surgery controls.
source: However, by day 14 and onwards they showed a strong FAA response, eventually having almost all of their daily activity preceding meal time as did sham surgery controls (Figure 10D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Dopamine signaling in the dorsal striatum is sufficient for acquisition of FAA.
source: From this experiment we conclude that dopamine signaling in the dorsal striatum is sufficient for acquisition of FAA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DD-VR experiment.

claim: WT mice exhibited a 24-hr rhythm of Per2 expression with peak expression at ZT 12 (lights-off), which is advanced by comparison with the daily rhythm previously reported in AL fed rodents.
source: WT mice exhibited a 24-hr rhythm with peak expression at ZT 12 (lights-off), which is advanced by comparison with the daily rhythm previously reported in AL fed rodents (e.g., Harbour et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 11 and comparison to prior research.

claim: D1R KO mice exhibited a markedly attenuated daily rhythm of striatal Per2 expression, due primarily to reduced expression at ZT 12.
source: KO mice exhibited a markedly attenuated daily rhythm of striatal Per2 expression, due primarily to reduced expression at ZT 12 (Figure 11).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 11.

claim: The daily rhythm of Per2 expression evident in the dorsal striatum of WT mice anticipating a daily meal is dependent on dopamine signaling at D1 receptors.
source: These results permit a substantive conclusion that the daily rhythm of Per2 expression evident in the dorsal striatum of WT mice anticipating a daily meal is dependent on dopamine signaling at D1 receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Per2 expression data.

claim: A 2-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of time of day (F(4,30) = 5.07, p = 0.0031), genotype (F(1,30) = 10.08, p = 0035), and interaction (F(4,30) = 22.02, p < 0.0001) in Per2 expression.
source: A 2-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of time of day (F(4,30) = 5.07, p = 0.0031), genotype (F(1,30) = 10.08, p = 0035), and interaction (F(4,30) = 22.02, p < 0.0001) in Per2 expression.
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the Per2 expression data.

claim: The immediate response to injection of SKF-81297 was observed as an increase in activity in caffeine and SKF-81297 mice that was more prolonged than that of water-injected controls.
source: The immediate response to injection was observed as an increase in activity in caffeine and SKF-81297 mice that was more prolonged than that of water-injected controls (Figure 12A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 12A.

claim: Water-injected mice showed a habituation to injection but caffeine-injected mice showed increased activity by day 12.
source: This trend continued through day 12, where water-injected mice showed a habituation to injection but caffeine-injected mice showed increased activity (Figure 12B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: On day 13, when no injection was performed, the SKF-injected mice showed increased activity compared to both water and caffeine-injected controls during the 3 hr after scheduled injection.
source: On day 13, when no injection was performed, leaving all mice undisturbed (no cage changes), the SKF-injected mice showed increased activity compared to both water and caffeine-injected controls during the 3 hr after scheduled injection (Figure 12C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: On day 0, there was no increase in activity preceding daily injection, as expected.
source: On day 0, there was no increase in activity preceding daily injection, as expected (Figure 12D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 12D.

claim: After 7 days of injection, there was a trend toward increased activity in SKF-injected mice that was not statistically significant (p = 0.0513, Kruskal–Wallis test).
source: After 7 days of injection, we observed a trend toward increased activity in SKF-injected mice that was not statistically significant (p = 0.0513, Kruskal–Wallis test) (Figure 12E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 12E.

claim: By days 12 and 13, the fraction of high activity of SKF-injected mice was significantly greater than either that of water- or caffeine-injected mice (day 12, SKF-81297 vs water, SKF 81297 vs caffeine [p < 0.01]; day 13, SKF 81297 vs water [p < 0.01], SKF-81297 vs caffeine [p < 0.01]).
source: By days 12 and 13, the fraction of high activity of SKF-injected mice was significantly greater than either that of water- or caffeine-injected mice (day 12, SKF-81297 vs water, SKF 81297 vs caffeine [p < 0.01]; day 13, SKF 81297 vs water [p < 0.01], SKF-81297 vs caffeine [p < 0.01]) (Figure 12F–H).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 12F-H.

claim: Timed activation of D1R neurons is sufficient to induce moderate behavioral entrainment (about 20% of total high activity behavior in a 3-hr pre-injection window).
source: From these experiments, we conclude that timed activation of D1R neurons is sufficient to induce moderate behavioral entrainment (about 20% of total high activity behavior in a 3-hr pre-injection window).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SKF-81297 injection experiments.

claim: Behavioral entrainment induced by timed D1R activation can persist in the absence of stimuli, as at the end of day 13 anticipatory activity occurs nearly 46 hr after the last injection of drug.
source: Moreover, this entrainment can persist in the absence of stimuli, as at the end of day 13 anticipatory activity occurs nearly 46 hr after the last injection of drug.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SKF-81297 injection experiments.

claim: Anticipation of a daily meal is markedly attenuated in mice lacking D1R.
source: In this study, we provide comprehensive evidence supporting an important role for dopamine signaling via D1R in the expression of FAA in CR mice fed in the light period. Using video-based automated behavior analysis, motion sensors, and running discs, we demonstrated that anticipation of a daily meal is markedly attenuated in mice lacking D1R.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Anticipation of a daily meal is normal in mice lacking D2R.
source: By contrast, it is normal in mice lacking D2R and in dopamine-deficient mice with local production of dopamine in the dorsal striatum.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Anticipation of a daily meal is normal in dopamine-deficient mice with local production of dopamine in the dorsal striatum.
source: By contrast, it is normal in mice lacking D2R and in dopamine-deficient mice with local production of dopamine in the dorsal striatum.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The reduction in FAA in D1R KO mice is evident both in total counts and when normalized for total daily activity.
source: The reduction in FAA in D1R KO mice is evident both in total counts and when normalized for total daily activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Attenuated FAA in D1R KO mice may involve three distinct processes: circadian oscillator entrainment, incentive motivation, and metabolic homeostasis.
source: We propose that attenuated FAA in D1R KO mice may involve three distinct processes; circadian oscillator entrainment, incentive motivation, and metabolic homeostasis.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings.

claim: Mammalian circadian clocks are comprised of populations of coupled circadian oscillators (clock cells).
source: Mammalian circadian clocks are comprised of populations of coupled circadian oscillators (clock cells) (Colwell, 2000; Mohawk and Takahashi, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Disruption of coupling within a population of circadian oscillators can flatten aggregate clock output and attenuate rhythm peaks.
source: Disruption of coupling within a population of circadian oscillators can flatten aggregate clock output and attenuate rhythm peaks.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian oscillators.

claim: A circadian oscillator entrainment interpretation of attenuated FAA in D1R KO mice is suggested by the marked attenuation of a daily rhythm of clock gene (Per2) expression in the dorsal striatum.
source: A circadian oscillator entrainment interpretation of attenuated FAA in D1R KO mice is suggested by two observations. First, in parallel with attenuated FAA rhythms, D1R KO mice also exhibited a marked attenuation of a daily rhythm of clock gene (Per2) expression in the dorsal striatum.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A circadian oscillator entrainment interpretation of attenuated FAA in D1R KO mice is suggested by the observation that a daily injection of the D1 agonist SKF-81257 was sufficient to induce a rhythm of anticipatory activity that was synchronized to the injection time and that persisted during a withdrawal day.
source: Second, a daily injection of the D1 agonist SKF-81257 was sufficient to induce a rhythm of anticipatory activity that was synchronized to the injection time and that persisted during a withdrawal day.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Dopamine signaling via D1R in the dorsal striatum entrains circadian oscillators that regulate the timing and amplitude of FAA.
source: These results converge on a hypothesis that dopamine signaling via D1R in the dorsal striatum entrains circadian oscillators that regulate the timing and amplitude of FAA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: A daily rhythm of dopamine release associated with food acquisition serves to coordinate the phase of circadian clock cells in the dorsal striatum.
source: We speculate that a daily rhythm of dopamine release associated with food acquisition serves to coordinate the phase of circadian clock cells in the dorsal striatum, and that genetic deletion of D1R impairs this function, thereby reducing the amplitude of the population rhythm and the magnitude of the activity rhythm driven by these oscillators.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Genetic deletion of D1R impairs the coordination of circadian clock cells in the dorsal striatum, thereby reducing the amplitude of the population rhythm and the magnitude of the activity rhythm driven by these oscillators.
source: We speculate that a daily rhythm of dopamine release associated with food acquisition serves to coordinate the phase of circadian clock cells in the dorsal striatum, and that genetic deletion of D1R impairs this function, thereby reducing the amplitude of the population rhythm and the magnitude of the activity rhythm driven by these oscillators.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: D1R signaling in food-entrainable oscillators of the dorsal striatum may be analogous to VPAC receptor signaling in the SCN, which is critical for coupling the population of circadian oscillators that constitute this light entrained circadian pacemaker.
source: In this respect, D1R signaling in food-entrainable oscillators of the dorsal striatum may be analogous to VPAC receptor signaling in the SCN, which is critical for coupling the population of circadian oscillators that constitute this light entrained circadian pacemaker (Harmar et al., 2002; Aton et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative analogy based on the findings and prior research.

claim: Circadian clocks directly drive or gate output of neural systems that produce observable daily rhythms of rest and activity.
source: Circadian clocks are thought to directly drive or gate output of neural systems that produce observable daily rhythms of rest and activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clocks.

claim: Circadian clocks generate internal time cues that animals can use to discriminate time of day; for example, to permit daily time-place learning, or time-compensated-sun-compass orientation.
source: Circadian clocks also generate internal time cues that animals can use to discriminate time of day; for example, to permit daily time-place learning, or time-compensated-sun-compass orientation (Mistlberger, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A representation of circadian clock phase, by repeated association with a fixed daily meal time, could acquire salience as an incentive stimulus and generate a daily rhythm of incentive motivation manifest as FAA.
source: A representation of circadian clock phase, by repeated association with a fixed daily meal time, could acquire salience as an incentive stimulus and generate a daily rhythm of incentive motivation manifest as FAA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: A model in which circadian clock phase acquires salience as an incentive stimulus could account for the ability of some animals to anticipate two or more meal times per day.
source: Such a model could account for the ability of some animals to anticipate two or more meal times per day (Biebach et al., 1991; Van der Zee et al., 2008; Luby et al., 2012; Mistlberger et al., 2012; Mulder et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attenuated FAA in D1R KO mice may reflect impaired incentive motivation, due to a failure to attribute incentive salience to representations of circadian phase, due to degradation of the clock signals by striatal oscillator damping, or both.
source: It is therefore possible that attenuated FAA in D1R KO mice, which did not express FAA even when aroused 2 hr prior to meal time (Figure 6), reflects impaired incentive motivation, due to a failure to attribute incentive salience to representations of circadian phase, due to degradation of the clock signals by striatal oscillator damping, or both.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Enhanced palatability can compensate for deficits in oscillator entrainment or incentive motivation in D1R KO mice, but this effect is masked by CR.
source: These observations suggest that enhanced palatability can compensate for deficits in oscillator entrainment or incentive motivation, but that this effect is masked by CR.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from the palatable meal experiments.

claim: The activity phenotype in D1R KO mice reflects an additional metabolic factor.
source: We speculate that the activity phenotype in D1R KO mice reflects an additional metabolic factor.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: D1R KO mice exhibited hyperactivity during acute food deprivation but were significantly less active throughout the day and night during chronic CR schedules.
source: Although D1R KO mice, like WT mice, exhibited hyperactivity during acute food deprivation they were significantly less active throughout the day and night during the chronic CR schedules.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the acute fasting and chronic CR experiments.

claim: During chronic restriction, D1R KO mice maintained nocturnal body temperatures relative to WT mice, which were hypothermic at night and early in the light period.
source: This was not due to metabolic collapse, given that during chronic restriction, D1R KO mice maintained nocturnal body temperatures relative to WT mice, which were hypothermic at night and early in the light period.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the body temperature experiments.

claim: WT mice may conserve energy by reducing metabolism at night and expend energy by raising body temperature and locomotor activity in anticipation of a regular daily meal time.
source: These results suggest a different strategy used by WT and KO mice to maintain metabolic homeostasis during CR. The WT mice may conserve energy by reducing metabolism at night and expend energy by raising body temperature and locomotor activity in anticipation of a regular daily meal time.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: D1R KO mice switch from an initial hyperactivity to a long-term hypoactivity of sufficient magnitude to support a more normal body temperature despite restricted calorie intake.
source: The KO mice, by contrast, switch from an initial hyperactivity to a long-term hypoactivity of sufficient magnitude to support a more normal body temperature despite restricted calorie intake.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The food anticipation phenotype in CR D1R KO mice may be explained by an alteration in the strategy to maintain metabolic homeostasis, which damps activity non-specifically throughout the 24-hr cycle and an impairment in circadian entrainment and/or incentive motivation processes that results in a disproportionate reduction of activity in anticipation of meal time.
source: Thus, the food anticipation phenotype in CR D1R KO mice may be explained by an alteration in the strategy to maintain metabolic homeostasis, which damps activity non-specifically throughout the 24-hr cycle and an impairment in circadian entrainment and/or incentive motivation processes that results in a disproportionate reduction of activity in anticipation of meal time.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings.

claim: Despite the marked attenuation of FAA in D1R KO mice, the preprandial rise in body temperature is essentially normal.
source: Another notable feature of the food entrainment phenotype in D1R KO mice is that despite the marked attenuation of FAA, the preprandial rise in body temperature is essentially normal (Figure 9).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Feeding schedules entrain circadian oscillators in many body tissues and brain regions.
source: Feeding schedules entrain circadian oscillators in many body tissues and brain regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about food entrainment.

claim: There is at present no direct evidence for a master food-entrainable pacemaker analogous to the retinorecipient light-entrainable pacemaker in the SCN, which in mammals is indispensible for entrainment to light:dark cycles.
source: There is at present no direct evidence for a master food-entrainable pacemaker analogous to the retinorecipient light-entrainable pacemaker in the SCN, which in mammals is indispensible for entrainment to light:dark cycles.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Hypophysectomy eliminates preprandial temperature increases but not FAA.
source: Indeed hypophysectomy eliminates preprandial temperature increases but not FAA (Davidson and Stephan, 1999), a dissociation that we have also observed with mice showing temperature entrainment without FAA (Gallardo et al., 2012) and mice showing FAA without showing preprandial temperature increases (Luby et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Food entrainment may involve multiple parallel entrainment pathways, acting on a fully distributed, non-hierarchical system of circadian oscillators in local circuits, each responsible for generating food-entrained rhythms in tissue specific functions.
source: Food entrainment may involve multiple parallel entrainment pathways, acting on a fully distributed, non-hierarchical system of circadian oscillators in local circuits, each responsible for generating food-entrained rhythms in tissue specific functions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings.

claim: The differential effect of the D1R KO on behavior and body temperature is consistent with a model of multiple parallel entrainment pathways in food entrainment.
source: The differential effect of the D1R KO on behavior and body temperature is consistent with this model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Evidence that daily rhythms of food anticipatory activity may reflect entrainment of circadian oscillations in the dorsal striatum by daily reward schedules and D1R signaling suggest new insights into the processes that may induce and sustain daily repetitive or even addictive behaviors.
source: Evidence that daily rhythms of food anticipatory activity may reflect entrainment of circadian oscillations in the dorsal striatum by daily reward schedules and D1R signaling suggest new insights into the processes that may induce and sustain daily repetitive or even addictive behaviors.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation of the findings to broader implications.
